newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil could double soy imports after record sales.
newsitem.headline: Brazil could double soy imports after record sales.

text.p: Brazil could double its soybean imports this year as crushers look abroad for supply after a harvest during which tax conditions and high prices encouraged growers to export as much as possible.

Some domestic industry sources think imports could reach two million tonnes this year and say that with expectations of a lower Argentine crop, they will be looking to the United States to provide much of the extra product.
"There are some firms which are already working with a figure of two million tonnes," said Cesar Borges de Souza, director of processor Caramuru Oleos Vegetais.

Brazil traditionally imports around one million tonnes of soybeans after the end of its harvesting and export season, most of it from Mercosur partners Paraguay and Argentina, said the Brazilian Association of Vegetable Oils Industries (Abiove).

"One million would normally come from Mercosur but if there is a sharp increase, the surplus would have to come from the U.S., there is no other worldwide supplier," said Abiove secretary general Fabio Trigueirinho.

Following the lifting of the ICMS export tax in September 1996, it became more profitable to export soybeans over soymeal and soyoil so that the domestic industry was left competing strongly for beans.

A peak in prices on the Chicago commodity futures exchange at the height of Brazil's soybean harvest in March and April meant 75 percent of this year's harvest has already been committed, according to independent consultant Safras e Mercado.
Exports are seen reaching up to 8.5 million tonnes in the 1997/98 marketing year (February-January), compared with 3.65 million in 1996/97 and 3.52 million in 1995/96.
Some processors say it is still to early to forecast what impact this level of foreign sales could have later on in the year.
"We still haven't finished exporting," said Borges de Souza, adding that his company was cautiously working with estimated total imports of 1.5 million tonnes.

"There are a lot of soybeans available in Paraguay so we have some doubt about whether that much needs to be imported from the U.S.," said Charles Van Der Heyde, director of external sales at Ceval Alimentos.

"I don't think Brazil will import as much from the U.S. as the market is expecting," he said, although he added, "We see Brazil importing between 700,000 and one million tonnes from the U.S. but no more than that."
